analysis.one_liner: Bans paid conversion therapy as consumer fraud, enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban commercial conversion therapy drew 219 House cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal offense for anyone to charge money for "conversion therapy" — any treatment that claims it can change a person's sexual orientation or gender identity — and to advertise such claims. It would be treated as an unfair or deceptive practice under the Federal Trade Commission Act, enforceable by the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general. The bill leaves untouched counseling that supports someone through a gender transition or simply helps a client explore their identity.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBTQ people, especially minors, whose families are targeted by paid conversion therapy. The bill's findings cite the professional consensus that the practice is ineffective and has been linked to depression, self-harm, low self-esteem, family rejection, and suicide; treating it as fraud would let federal and state enforcers shut it down and penalize anyone selling or advertising it. Parents paying for it for their children would also be protected as consumers of a fraudulent service.
analysis.who_benefits_short: LGBTQ people targeted by conversion therapy

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for anyone to provide conversion therapy for payment, or to advertise that it can change someone's sexual orientation or gender identity or that it is harmless — and defines conversion therapy broadly to cover efforts to change behaviors and expressions as well as attractions.

Enforces the ban through the existing consumer-protection system: violations are treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, so the FTC, the Attorney General, and state attorneys general can all bring civil actions and seek penalties.

Rests the ban on Congress's formal findings that being LGBTQ is not a disorder, that no scientific evidence supports conversion therapy, and that the practice has been shown to contribute to depression, self-harm, and suicide — framing it as fraud on families who pay for it.

Carves out legitimate care: the ban does not reach counseling that assists someone undergoing a gender transition or that provides acceptance, support, and identity exploration, including sexual-orientation-neutral interventions.

analysis.who_pays: Practitioners who sell conversion therapy — counseling operations and individual providers that charge for it — would lose their ability to collect fees for it and would face FTC penalties and lawsuits. Anyone advertising it with claims that it works or is safe would also be exposed to enforcement. Federal agencies and state attorneys general would bear modest enforcement costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Conversion therapy providers and their advertisers

drawbacks.text: Regulating talk therapy raises free-speech questions, and the bill's own text acknowledges this by exempting any product or service protected by the First Amendment — a carve-out that critics could argue leaves much of the practice beyond the ban's reach.

The bill gives enforcement power only to the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general; individuals harmed by conversion therapy would have no right to sue on their own behalf under this law.
Enforcement would arrive after the fact through civil actions rather than up front: providers could keep operating until an agency or state attorney general successfully sues them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete for a group at documented risk of serious harm: a nationwide ban on selling and advertising a practice the mental-health professions have found ineffective and dangerous. The costs fall almost entirely on the small industry that sells conversion therapy, plus modest enforcement expenses. The design is narrower than a criminal ban — it leans on fraud law, exempts First Amendment-protected speech, and gives victims no private right of action — but those limits also make it more defensible in court. On balance, a well-targeted consumer-protection measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, passed to a subcommittee the next day, and then sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on June 27, 2019, with 64 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On June 28, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce — the last action ever taken on it.
Support kept growing: it eventually had 219 cosponsors, all of them Democrats — 219 of the chamber's 231 House Democrats — with no Republican cosponsor.
The Energy and Commerce Committee never held a hearing or marked up the bill, and the House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Conversion therapy providers, who remain free to sell and advertise the practice under federal law, since no ban was ever enacted. Politically, the bill's cosponsors got to record support without forcing a vote that could have tested it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Conversion therapy providers, who kept operating

for.name: Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 64 original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 219 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it one of the most widely backed measures never to reach the floor.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the 219 cosponsors was a Democrat — 219 of the House's 231 Democrats — and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no one ever had to cast one.

industries.note: The bill would make it a federal unfair practice to charge for conversion therapy or advertise that it can change someone's orientation or gender identity, cutting off the revenue stream of providers who sell it and exposing them to FTC penalties and lawsuits. Its profit depends on selling families a service the mental-health professions have found ineffective and harmful.

Much commercial conversion therapy is delivered through religiously affiliated counseling programs; the bill defines 'person' to include any corporation, association, or entity, so those operations would fall under the same advertising and compensation ban.
